nodes.summary: The distinguishing advantage of a distinguisher $D$ between encryptions of the messages $m$ and $m'$ is $\lvert \Pr[D \text{ outputs } 1 \text{ on } m] - \Pr[D \text{ outputs } 1 \text{ on } m'] \rvert$, the two probabilities being those of the indistinguishability experiment for $m$ and for $m'$.
nodes.title: Distinguishing advantage between encryptions

nodes.summary: Let $S$ be a public-key encryption scheme with key generation $\mathrm{Gen}$ and probabilistic encryption $\mathrm{Enc}$. For a distribution of random coins on a type $R$, a distinguisher $D$, which maps a public key, a ciphertext and coins to a bit, and a message $m$, the indistinguishability experiment draws a key pair $(pk, sk) \leftarrow \mathrm{Gen}$, coins $r$ and a ciphertext…
nodes.title: The indistinguishability experiment

nodes.summary: Let $\varepsilon \ge 0$. If a public-key scheme is semantically secure with error $\varepsilon$, already for trivial a priori information and Boolean guesses, then it has indistinguishable encryptions with error $2\varepsilon$.
nodes.title: Semantic security implies indistinguishability, all-adversary form

nodes.summary: A public-key encryption scheme, with a length function on its messages and a distribution of the adversary's coins, has indistinguishable encryptions with error $\varepsilon$ if for every distinguisher $D$ (a function of the public key, the ciphertext and the coins) and all messages $m, m'$ of the same length, the distinguishing advantage of $D$ between encryptions of $m$ and $m'$ is at most $\varepsilon$.
nodes.title: Indistinguishability of encryptions with error `ε`

nodes.summary: Let a public-key scheme be correct, and let $m \ne m'$ be messages of the same length. Then for every distribution of coins and every $\varepsilon < 1$, the scheme does not have indistinguishable encryptions with error $\varepsilon$ in this concrete model. The distinguisher that outputs $1$ exactly when some secret key matching the public key decrypts the ciphertext to $m'$ outputs $1$ on every encryption of $m'$…
nodes.title: Indistinguishability is unattainable against unbounded distinguishers

nodes.summary: Under the hypotheses of unattainability of indistinguishability, a correct public-key scheme is not semantically secure with any error $\varepsilon < \tfrac12$, already for trivial a priori information and Boolean targets: semantic security with error $\varepsilon$ would give indistinguishability with error $2\varepsilon < 1$.
nodes.title: Semantic security is unattainable against unbounded adversaries

nodes.summary: For an eavesdropper whose two challenge messages $(m_0, m_1)$ do not depend on the public key or on its coins, the framework's left-or-right eavesdropping experiment $\mathsf{PubK}^{\mathrm{eav}}$ with challenge bit $b$ is the indistinguishability experiment on $m_b$, with the eavesdropper's guess as distinguisher.
nodes.title: `PubK^eav` with fixed messages is the indistinguishability experiment

nodes.summary: Let $\varepsilon \ge 0$ and suppose that a public-key scheme has indistinguishable encryptions with error $\varepsilon$ and that for each length $n$ of a message there is a dummy message of length $n$. Then the scheme is semantically secure with error $\varepsilon$, for any types of a priori information and of guesses, with the simulator as ideal adversary.
nodes.title: Indistinguishability implies semantic security, all-adversary form

nodes.summary: A public-key encryption scheme, with a length function on its messages and a distribution of the adversary's coins, is semantically secure with error $\varepsilon$ (for a priori information in a type $H$ and guesses in a type $T$) if for every adversary $A$ there is an ideal adversary $A'$ such that for every plaintext distribution $X$, every function $h$ and every target function $f$, the probability that $A$ wins…
nodes.title: Semantic security with error `ε`

nodes.summary: Given an adversary $A$ and a dummy message $\mathrm{dummy}(n)$ for each length $n$, the simulator, on a length $n$ and a priori information $v$, draws a key pair, coins $r$ and a ciphertext $c \leftarrow \mathrm{Enc}_{pk}(\mathrm{dummy}(n))$, and outputs $A(pk, c, v, r)$. It runs $A$ once on an encryption of a dummy message instead of the real plaintext; Goldreich uses $1^{|\alpha|}$ as the dummy.
nodes.title: The simulator of Goldreich's Proposition 5.2.6

nodes.summary: For an adversary $A$, functions $h$ and $f$ and a plaintext $x$, this distinguisher maps a public key $pk$, a ciphertext $c$ and coins $r$ to the bit $[A(pk, c, h(x), r) = f(x)]$. The values $h(x)$ and $f(x)$ are built in, which is why no computability assumption on $h$ or $f$ is needed.
nodes.title: The distinguisher hardwiring one plaintext

nodes.summary: For a length function on messages, an ideal adversary $A'$ (which maps a length and a priori information to a distribution of guesses), a plaintext distribution $X$, an a priori information function $h$ and a target function $f$, the experiment draws $x \leftarrow X$, then a guess $t \leftarrow A'(|x|, h(x))$, and outputs whether $t = f(x)$. The ideal adversary sees neither the public key nor a ciphertext.
nodes.title: The ideal semantic-security experiment

nodes.summary: For a public-key encryption scheme, a distribution of coins, an adversary $A$ (a function of the public key, a ciphertext, a priori information and coins, with values in a type $T$ of guesses), a plaintext distribution $X$, an a priori information function $h$ and a target function $f$, the experiment draws $x \leftarrow X$, a key pair, coins $r$ and a ciphertext $c \leftarrow \mathrm{Enc}_{pk}(x)$, and outputs…
nodes.title: The real semantic-security experiment

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be an adversary, $X$ a plaintext distribution, $h$ and $f$ functions on plaintexts and $\varepsilon \ge 0$. Suppose that for every plaintext $x$ in the support of $X$ the distinguisher hardwiring $x$ has advantage at most $\varepsilon$ between encryptions of $x$ and of the dummy message of length $|x|$. nodes.title: Indistinguishability implies semantic security, per adversary

nodes.summary: Let $D$ be a distinguisher and $m \ne m'$ two messages of the same length. Take the two-point distribution on $m$ and $m'$ as plaintext distribution, no a priori information, and the target function $f(x) = [x = m']$. Let $A$ be the adversary that outputs $D(pk, c, r)$. Then for every ideal adversary $A'$, the probabilities being those of the real and ideal experiments and of the indistinguishability experiments…

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
